primary_claim: Linear probes trained on Gemma-3-27B activations predict the model's revealed task preferences (0.86 Pearson within-topic, 0.82 cross-topic) and track out-of-distribution preference shifts induced by system prompts and role-playing personas, with steering along the probe direction producing a weak but statistically significant causal shift (~17%) in choice probability.

effect.metric: Pearson correlation between probe predictions and fitted task-preference utilities; steering effect on choice probability
effect.value: 0.86 within-topic / 0.82 cross-topic (Gemma-3-27B instruct); steering at +/-3% activation norm shifts P(choose task) by ~17%, random-direction control ~0% (SD=2.3)

stated_future_work: Investigate why steering effects are modest and what other mechanistic determinants of revealed preferences exist
Study how persona-relative these representations are, e.g. using dimensionality reduction to map persona space across layers
Determine whether base (pre-trained) models have evaluative representations from pre-training or these are produced by post-training
limitations_stated: Causal evidence from steering is weak; effects are modest (~17%) and only on already-borderline tasks
Pairwise accuracy is capped at ~87% because Thurstonian utility estimates are a noisy fit to choice data
Open-ended generation steering experiments used a small sample and found no strong measurable effect
quote: We find that these generalise ood to system-prompt induced preference shifts, including via personas.
